record.passage: Chen had the whole spring break mapped out on the whiteboard in his Vancouver bedroom. Monday: all of algebra. Tuesday: all of geometry. Wednesday: statistics, then free days. "Exams are in two weeks. I'll be done by Wednesday and gaming by Thursday," he told Oskar over the phone. Oskar laughed. "You said that at Christmas." "Christmas was different. My cousins were visiting." By Wednesday night, Chen was still on algebra. Every practice set took twice as long as the answers at the back made it look. On Thursday morning he stared at the whiteboard, marker in hand, feeling almost betrayed by it. Three topics, one done. He wiped off 'free days' and started again, with Oskar's Christmas warning ringing in his ears.

qa.a: By Wednesday night, Chen was still on algebra.

qa.a: He had trusted the bright picture on it, and real work taking twice as long felt like the plan had let him down.

record.grounding: A teenager maps a whole maths syllabus into three days, ignores his Christmas experience, and is shocked when algebra alone fills all three.

The Independence Day function at the government school in Nabha ended at noon, and by evening Amandeep, fifteen, was still thinking about it. She had recited her Punjabi poem in front of the whole village. The sarpanch had shaken her hand. Her teacher had said, "You made me cry." Jatin had shouted "Superstar!" from the back.
But while she was walking off the stage, a boy near the tractor trolleys had called out, "Slow down, grandma, it's not a funeral," and a few people laughed.
That line played in her head as she fed the buffaloes. It played again at dinner. Two days later, when Jatin said, "Everyone's still talking about your poem," she said, "Yeah, about how boring I was."
"What? No!"
She shrugged and went inside. She had already decided not to enter the district competition.

qa.a: Jatin shouted "Superstar!" from the back.

qa.a: The comment felt like a threat to how people see her, so her mind keeps replaying it, while the handshake, the teacher's tears and Jatin's cheering feel easy to shrug off.

qa.a: Jatin is likely confused and hurt for her, since he knows the praise was real and can't understand why one stranger's joke counts more.

record.passage: I'm Vaibhav, and as a boy of nine I feared every dog in the world. It started when my cousin Indu told me about a boy at her school who got bitten by a stray. record.passage:
Another coffee, Ujjwal? Sit. Let Parveen aunty tell you something. When I was nineteen, in my second year at Aligarh, a magazine in the reading room said coffee drinkers live longer. I had never liked coffee, but I started drinking it with every meal. I told my roommates it was for my health. I really believed each cup was adding years to my life.
Then my statistics professor brought that same article to class. He asked us, "Who drinks coffee in this country?" People with a bit of money, office jobs, time to sit in coffee houses. People with healthier lives for many reasons. And people who are already unwell often give coffee up. The coffee wasn't the reason; it was riding along with other things. I felt so foolish. So drink your coffee because you like it, not because a headline told you to.

qa.a: In a magazine in the reading room, in her second year at Aligarh.

qa.q: Why did Parveen start drinking coffee with every meal though she never liked it?

qa.q: What question did the professor ask, and why does it help?
qa.a: He asked who drinks coffee in the country, which brought out hidden factors like money, office jobs and free time that could explain longer lives.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal take this story from Parveen aunty?
qa.a: Ujjwal might feel gently teased about the coffee, but also see that she is sharing her own mistake so he won't trust headlines too quickly.

At stand-up he'd say, "Great, love that," in a voice that meant the opposite. I had been team lead for two months, and he had been passed over for the post.

Yamini, I see you've written "SHOULD WORK HARDER" on your monitor in red. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age at this same office.

At twenty-five, Ramesh here was a skinny young man with a notebook that said, on every page: "You must be more productive." Every evening I read it and felt like a failure. The more I read it, the less I did. I'd sit at my desk feeling guilty and then go home having done nothing but feel guilty.

One day my old boss, Mrs D'Costa, read it over my shoulder. She said, "Who wants to work for someone who shouts at them all day? Not even you."

So I changed one line. "I'd like to be more productive. Today: finish the Kolhapur file before tea."

It sounds silly. But I finished the file. And the next day I wrote another small one.

So maybe, Yamini, take off the red note. Try "I'd like to" and one thing.

The only signal in Hansa's village came near the water tank behind the panchayat office, so that's where she stood at dusk, phone held high. The college group had 212 members, and tonight it was all about Arohi's speech from English Day: her voice shaking on the word 'responsibility', cut into a loop with a goat bleating.
Laughing faces, then more. Hansa scrolled. Surely Manpreet, the class rep, would say something. Or one of the toppers. Someone.
Twenty minutes passed. Nobody did. The loop had been shared into another group.
Her mother called from the courtyard that the rotis were getting cold.
Hansa typed, deleted, typed again: 'Arohi practised this for a week. It's not funny to me. Please take the loop down.'
She sent it and went in to eat. When she came back to the tank, four people had written 'agreed', and the loop was gone.

qa.a: She goes near the water tank behind the panchayat office.

qa.q: What was Hansa thinking during the twenty minutes of scrolling?
qa.a: She kept expecting someone else, Manpreet the class rep or one of the toppers, to speak up; with 212 members it felt as if it could not be her job.

qa.q: Which choice changed the group chat, and why did it work?
qa.a: Hansa's short, calm message naming Arohi's effort and asking for the loop to go; once one person spoke, four others agreed and the loop was taken down.

qa.a: Before, Arohi would have watched laughing faces pile up with nobody on her side; after, she could see that at least five people did not find it funny, and the loop was gone.

I'm Jagdish, and last summer in our railway colony I had a rule: no playing with the Line kids. They lived in the huts by the tracks, and I told everyone they were jungli and dirty. So when their ball bounced into our lane, I kicked it into the drain. 'They're used to muck,' I said. 'They won't mind.'
My cousin Preeti fished it out and walked it back to them. I was angry with her.
The next day I saw a girl from the huts, Sulochana, crying by the drain and washing that ball with her hands. It was her birthday ball, Preeti told me.
I didn't feel like a winner. I felt small.
Now I say their names. Sulochana bowls better than me.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Jagdish, and what changed after it?
qa.a: Seeing Sulochana crying and washing her birthday ball; Jagdish felt small, dropped the 'jungli' label and started using the children's names.

qa.a: Preeti treated them as ordinary children whose ball mattered, so she fished it out and took it back; to her they were simply neighbours.

record.passage:
In my first winter in Dublin, I was a number more often than a name. At the immigration office I was 'fifty-eight'. At the accommodation desk I was 'another non-EU one', said to a colleague as if I couldn't hear. A tutor once sighed that international students 'take up all the help'. I started keeping my coat on in seminars, as if I might be asked to leave.
What pulled me back was small. My lab partner Thomas said 'Morning, Noor' every single day, and asked what I thought about the results before he wrote anything down. On Sundays I called my cousin in Lucknow, who laughed at all my stories.
I still flinch when I hear 'fifty-eight'. But I learned to spend more of my time with the people who say my name.

qa.q: What number was Noor called at the immigration office?
qa.a: Fifty-eight.

qa.q: What does keeping a coat on in seminars suggest about how Noor felt?
qa.a: It suggests Noor felt unwelcome and temporary, like a burden who might be asked to leave, rather than a student who belonged.

qa.q: What choice helped Noor through that winter?
qa.a: Noor chose to spend more time with people who used Noor's name, Thomas in the lab and the cousin on Sunday calls; those ties pushed back against feeling like a number.

qa.q: How might Thomas's daily 'Morning, Noor' have looked from Thomas's side?
qa.a: For Thomas it was probably ordinary politeness and teamwork, asking a partner's view first; he may not have known how much it meant to someone treated as a number elsewhere.

I'm Ranjana. Last month at the team lunch, Gulnaz rolled her eyes about the new interns from the small-town colleges. 'Copy-paste machines. No brains, no English, just attendance.' People laughed. I almost did.
Instead I asked, 'Which one? Tell me about one of them.'
Gulnaz paused. 'Well... Mohit, the tall one.'
'What's Mohit like?'
'He comes in at eight because the bus from his village is the only one.' She stirred her dal. 'He asked me how to write a proper email. Twice.'
'Did he get it right the second time?'
She almost smiled. 'Better than some of us.'
The next week I saw her at Mohit's desk, going through his draft line by line. I think about that often. The whole group was easy to sneer at. One boy with a bus timetable wasn't.

For two weeks I have heard Gurpreet and two friends make comments about Mohit's voice and the way he walks. Today, after Mohit left lunch early again, I asked Gurpreet to stay back. record.passage: I'm Gopika, and I run the second-hand book stall at our college gate with Arnab. I can only tell you what I've seen, not what's in his head. In June he bought forty copies of an old-syllabus exam guide cheap, sure they'd sell. They didn't. The syllabus had changed. Every week I say, "Let's sell them to the raddi shop and use the shelf."
